name: Lord of the Flies
blurb: William Golding's novel of schoolboys stranded on an island who descend into savagery
title: Lord of the Flies Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Lord of the Flies summary: Ralph, Piggy, Jack and the conch, the beast, what happens chapter by chapter, the ending explained, themes and symbols.
h1: Lord of the Flies: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Lord of the Flies is the first novel by the British writer William Golding, published in 1954. During a war, a plane carrying a group of British schoolboys crashes on an uninhabited tropical island, and no adults survive. The boys try to govern themselves, electing a leader and making rules, while also hunting, playing and keeping a signal fire alight for rescue. The novel follows how fear, rivalry and the pull of violence break their small society apart.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: A fair-haired, athletic twelve-year-old who is elected chief
A plump, short-sighted boy with glasses, clever and practical, often mocked
The proud, aggressive leader of a group of choirboys who become hunters
A quiet, kind boy who often goes off alone and is prone to fainting fits
A secretive older boy among Jack's choir
Identical twins, known together as Samneric, who stay close to Ralph
The youngest boys, about six years old, who spend their days playing
A British officer who appears in the final chapter

body: Chapters 1–3: the assembly and the fire. After the crash, Ralph meets Piggy on the beach, and they find a large conch shell. Ralph blows it to call the scattered boys together, and Jack arrives leading his choir in black cloaks. The boys elect Ralph chief; to keep the peace, Ralph puts Jack in charge of the choir as hunters. Whoever holds the conch may speak at assemblies. Using Piggy's glasses to focus sunlight, they light a signal fire on the mountain, but it spreads out of control, and a small boy with a birthmark who had spoken of a snake-like beastie is never seen again. Ralph struggles to get shelters built while Jack thinks only of hunting.

Chapters 4–6: the missed ship and the beast. Jack's hunters paint their faces and kill a pig, but let the signal fire go out just as a ship passes. Ralph is furious, and when Piggy protests Jack hits him and breaks one lens of his glasses. Fear of a beast spreads among the boys. One night a dead airman from an air battle overhead drifts down by parachute onto the mountain. Sam and Eric, tending the fire, mistake him for the beast, and when Ralph, Jack and Roger climb up in the dark, they too flee in terror.

Chapters 7–9: the split and Simon's death. Jack calls an assembly to remove Ralph as chief, loses, and leaves to form his own tribe; most of the older boys gradually join him. The hunters kill a sow and leave its head on a sharpened stick as a gift for the beast. Simon, alone in a clearing, faces the fly-covered head, the Lord of the Flies, and in a trance it seems to speak to him, saying the beast cannot be hunted because it is part of the boys themselves. Simon then climbs the mountain, finds the dead parachutist and frees his lines. He runs down to tell the others, but at night, during a storm, Jack's tribe is chanting and dancing on the beach, with Ralph and Piggy among them. Simon crawls out of the forest and the boys, taking him for the beast, beat him to death. The tide carries his body out to sea.

Chapters 10–12: Castle Rock and the hunt. Jack's tribe now lives at a rocky stronghold, Castle Rock. They raid Ralph's camp at night and steal Piggy's glasses, their only means of making fire. Ralph, Piggy and the twins go to demand them back. Roger levers a boulder down from above; it strikes Piggy, shatters the conch and throws him onto the rocks below, killing him. The twins are captured and forced to join the tribe. Ralph escapes, and that night Sam and Eric warn him that the tribe will hunt him the next day and that Roger has sharpened a stick at both ends.

The hunters spread across the island, and Jack sets the forest on fire to drive Ralph out. Ralph runs until he falls on the beach at the feet of a British naval officer, whose ship has come because it saw the smoke. The officer takes the painted, spear-carrying boys for children playing a game and is disappointed to hear that two of them have been killed, remarking that British boys should have done better. Ralph breaks down and weeps for the loss of innocence, the darkness he has found in human beings and his friend Piggy, and the other boys cry with him. The embarrassed officer turns to look at his warship.

The rescue happens by accident: the fire that was meant to kill Ralph is the signal that saves him. Readers often stress the irony that the officer who scolds the boys is himself fighting a war, so the adult world is doing the same thing on a larger scale. Golding described the idea as a story about boys who behave the way real children would, in contrast to the well-behaved castaways of older adventure books, and the novel's own logic points to the beast being something inside the boys rather than on the island. Other readings put more weight on circumstances, such as fear, lack of adult authority and Jack's leadership.

ul: Civilisation and savagery: the conch, assemblies and rules give way to face paint, chanting and murder.
The beast within: the monster the boys fear does not exist, and Simon's vision suggests that the real danger is their own capacity for cruelty.
Order and power: Ralph's elected leadership loses out to Jack, who offers meat, excitement and protection from fear in return for obedience.
Symbols: the conch stands for democratic order, Piggy's glasses for reason and the power to make fire, the signal fire for hope of rescue, and the pig's head for the evil the boys create.
Loss of innocence: by the end even Ralph has taken part in violence, and his tears mark what all the boys have lost.
Length: a short novel of twelve chapters, usually around 200–230 pages; Golding received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1983.

Background: Golding wrote it partly as a reply to R. M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island (1857), in which shipwrecked boys behave well; film versions appeared in 1963 (directed by Peter Brook) and 1990 (directed by Harry Hook).
Content: violence between children, including two killings, a graphic pig hunt and bullying.
What teachers usually ask about: what the conch, glasses, fire and the Lord of the Flies symbolise; why Simon and Piggy die; Ralph and Jack as leaders; and the irony of the ending.

check.q: What object gives a boy the right to speak at assemblies?
check.why: Whoever holds the conch may speak; it is shattered when Piggy dies.

check.q: What is the beast the boys see on the mountain?
options: A shadow cast by the fire
The body of a dead airman with a parachute
check.why: A pilot killed in an air battle lands on the mountain, and his parachute makes the body seem to move.

check.q: Why does the navy ship come to the island at the end?
options: Ralph lights a new signal fire
It sees the smoke from the fire Jack starts to hunt Ralph
The ship has been searching for the crash site
check.why: The fire set to drive Ralph out draws the officer ashore.

faq.q: What does the title Lord of the Flies mean?
faq.a: It is the name the novel gives to the pig's head on a stick, swarming with flies, that the hunters leave as an offering to the beast. The phrase is a translation of Beelzebub, a name for a devil, linking the head to the evil inside the boys.

When Ralph and Piggy go to Castle Rock to ask for Piggy's stolen glasses, Roger deliberately pushes a large boulder down from above. It hits Piggy, smashes the conch he is holding and knocks him off the cliff onto the rocks by the sea, where he dies.

faq.q: Who killed Simon in Lord of the Flies?
faq.a: The boys kill him together during a frenzied dance in a storm, mistaking him for the beast as he crawls out of the forest. Ralph and Piggy are also in the circle, and afterwards both are ashamed.
